name: Tecaxic-Calixtlahuaca Roman head
hook: A Roman-style clay head in a 15th-century Aztec grave, resting on a thin, disputed 1933 dig record.
claim: Hristov and Genovés argued that a small terracotta head from a pre-Hispanic burial at Calixtlahuaca is a genuine 2nd-3rd century Roman artifact, and that its presence is the first solid evidence of transoceanic contact between the Old World and Mesoamerica before Columbus.

claimed_age.label: ~1780 ± 400 BP (TL, as reported 1999)
claimed_age.basis: Thermoluminescence on the ceramic, Forschungsstelle Archäometrie, Heidelberg (tested 1995), as published by Hristov & Genovés (1999). The lab later said this figure and its cited reference were incorrect.

accepted_age.label: ~870 BC-AD 1270 (corrected TL range, wide 2-sigma)
accepted_age.basis: Corrected TL range from the same Heidelberg lab (Schaaf & Wagner 2001); a standard TL determination wasn't possible. Excludes Colonial-period manufacture but too imprecise to confirm or exclude Roman origin.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: No accepted evidence existed for Old World-Mesoamerica contact before Columbus; only Norse contact in northeast North America (~AD 1000) was accepted.

unambiguous_signal.note: The head is unambiguously a human-made ceramic artifact; the dispute is over its origin and how it entered the deposit, not whether it is artificial.

documented_context.note: Reportedly found under floors of a structure per García Payón's field record, unpublished until decades after the 1933 dig; an unresolved allegation says the piece was planted as a prank.

multiple_dating_methods.note: Only thermoluminescence was applied to the head itself; the reported 1476-1510 burial date rests on stylistic/stratigraphic association with grave goods, not an independent physical date on the head.

multiple_labs.note: All TL work on the head was done at one laboratory (Forschungsstelle Archäometrie, Heidelberg).

professional_recovery.note: Reportedly excavated by José García Payón, a professional Mexican archaeologist, during a documented dig.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Published in Ancient Mesoamerica (Cambridge), followed by a peer-reviewed critique-and-reply exchange within two years.

material_accessible.note: The head was directly tested by an outside TL laboratory (Schaaf & Wagner) and, reportedly, examined by an outside Roman-art specialist.

independent_teams.note: An independent TL laboratory (Schaaf & Wagner, Heidelberg) and, reportedly, an outside Roman-art historian both examined the piece within the claim's first years.

proponent_stake.note: No documented commercial, religious or nationalist motive found. Hristov's research focuses on trans-oceanic contact questions — an ordinary specialization, not a clear unusual stake.

objections.text: The thermoluminescence figure Hristov and Genovés reported (1780 ± 400 BP) and its cited reference were incorrect; a standard TL age could not actually be obtained.
objections.raised_by: Peter Schaaf and Günther A. Wagner (the Heidelberg TL laboratory)
objections.outcome_note: Confirmed by the dating lab itself; Hristov and Genovés's own reply restates a corrected, much wider range (870 BC-AD 1270) rather than defending the original figure.

objections.text: Even a genuine ancient Roman object could have reached Mexico long after manufacture, e.g. as an early Colonial-period import, since TL only dates firing, not when the object entered the ground.
objections.raised_by: unnamed critics, per Hristov & Genovés's own reply
objections.outcome_note: Proponents call post-1492 import 'highly unlikely' given Aztec-Matlatzinca political relations, but no independent re-examination of the deposit has been published since.

objections.text: Provenance rests only on García Payón's field notes, reportedly unpublished until 1960; an archaeologist (Paul Schmidt) later reported an informal claim that a colleague planted the head as a prank during the dig.
objections.outcome_note: Per a tertiary account, Hristov calls the allegation hearsay, unconfirmable since those involved have died; García Payón's son disputes that his father was ever absent from the site.

objections.text: A single isolated find is a weak basis for inferring transoceanic contact; no other confirmed Roman-period Old World material is reported from a secure pre-Columbian Mesoamerican context.
objections.outcome_note: Schaaf and Wagner's own corrected TL range is, by their own statement, too imprecise to serve as central evidence for the contact claim either way.

objections.text: The Roman, Severan-period stylistic identification is reported as resting on one outside expert's opinion; it has not been independently replicated in published work by other Roman-art specialists.
objections.outcome_note: No second published art-historical assessment of the piece was found in the sources checked for this record.

status_note: Unresolved since 2001. The TL date is far less precise than first reported; the hoax allegation and a post-Columbian-import scenario remain neither confirmed nor excluded. No new dating or documentary study is on record since.

timeline.event: José García Payón reportedly excavates a burial at Tecaxic-Calixtlahuaca; a terracotta head is recovered among rich grave goods.
García Payón reportedly first publishes information about the head, decades after the excavation.
The head is thermoluminescence-tested at the Forschungsstelle Archäometrie, Heidelberg.
Hristov and Genovés publish the claim in Ancient Mesoamerica, presenting the TL date and arguing for Roman origin and transoceanic contact.
Schaaf and Wagner publish a correction: the reported TL figure and its reference were wrong; the real range is much wider.
Hristov and Genovés reply, restating corrected TL limits and addressing the post-Columbian-import and 'planted' hoax objections.

decisive_tests.test: Independently re-date the head (TL or OSL) at a second laboratory, with full raw equivalent-dose data published.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether an independent lab reproduces a Roman-era-consistent firing date or the wide, imprecise range Schaaf and Wagner report.

decisive_tests.test: Petrographic and chemical (e.g. pXRF or INAA) sourcing of the ceramic fabric against Roman Mediterranean and central Mexican clay/temper reference groups.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the clay is consistent with Mediterranean manufacture or with a local/regional Mexican fabric.

decisive_tests.test: Independent stylistic re-examination of the head by two or more Roman-art specialists, with published high-resolution imaging.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the Severan-period Roman identification is replicated by other experts rather than resting on one assessment.

decisive_tests.test: Archival review of García Payón's original 1933 field notes and any excavation photographs, plus documentary research on the Schmidt/Moedano planting allegation.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether contemporary records support an undisturbed, sealed context, and whether the hoax allegation has any documentary support beyond hearsay.

falsifier: Undermined if the fabric matches local or Colonial-period clay, or if documents confirm the planting allegation. Strengthened by an independent second TL/OSL date and petrographic sourcing to Mediterranean clays.

sources.citation: Hristov, R. & Genovés, S. (1999). Mesoamerican evidence of pre-Columbian transoceanic contacts. Ancient Mesoamerica 10(2): 207-213.
sources.note: Abstract read via lookup (Crossref/OpenAlex); states the 1995 TL test, the 1780±400 BP figure, and that context review found no sign of post-Columbian intrusion. Full text paywalled.

sources.citation: Schaaf, P. & Wagner, G.A. (2001). Comments on "Mesoamerican evidence of pre-Columbian transoceanic contacts" by Hristov and Genovés, in Ancient Mesoamerica 10:207-213, 1999. Ancient Mesoamerica 12(1): 79-81.
sources.note: Abstract read: the 1999 TL figure and reference were wrong; corrected range 870 BC-AD 1270, too imprecise to argue origin. Written by the analysts who ran the original test. Full text paywalled.

sources.citation: Hristov, R.H. & Genovés T., S. (2001). Reply to Peter Schaaf and Günther A. Wagner's "Comments on 'Mesoamerican evidence of pre-Columbian transoceanic contacts'". Ancient Mesoamerica 12(1): 83-86.
sources.note: Abstract read: restates corrected TL limits (2870-730 BP) and addresses two objections: post-1492 import, and the head being 'planted' during excavation. Full text paywalled.

sources.citation: Huster, A.C. & Smith, M.E. (2015). A new archaeological chronology for Aztec-period Calixtlahuaca, Mexico. Latin American Antiquity 26(1): 3-25.
sources.note: Abstract read: site occupied ca. AD 1100-1530 (final phase AD 1450-1530), consistent with the head's reported burial date. Does not discuss the head. Full text paywalled.

sources.citation: Smith, M.E., Borejsza, A., Huster, A. & Frederick, C.D. et al. (2013). Aztec period houses and terraces at Calixtlahuaca: the changing morphology of a Mesoamerican hilltop urban center. Journal of Field Archaeology 38(3): 227-243.
sources.note: Abstract read for site background (occupation ca. AD 1100-1530); does not discuss the head. Full text paywalled.

sources.citation: Wikipedia contributors. "Tecaxic-Calixtlahuaca head." Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia (revision accessed 2026-09-23).
sources.note: Tertiary source. Its 1933/1960 dates, Andreae ID, and the Schmidt/Moedano hoax claim trace to a since-offline Hristov & Genovés essay; not independently confirmed in peer-reviewed literature.

confidence_note: Claim-critique-reply chain (S1-S3) verified via checked abstracts; full texts stayed paywalled. Provenance/hoax details rest on one tertiary source (S6) tracing to an inaccessible primary essay.
corrections: Brief: TL dating 'reported by Hristov & Genovés (1999) as pre-Columbian.' The lab itself (Schaaf & Wagner 2001) found that figure wrong; the corrected range (870 BC-AD 1270) is far wider and too imprecise to argue origin.

Brief names 'Michael E. Smith' as a critic questioning provenance. No Smith publication on this case was located despite searching; the verified critique is Schaaf & Wagner (2001). Smith's role is UNVERIFIED here.
notes: The head is reportedly a fragment (face/head only) of a larger figurine, found with gold, copper, turquoise, rock crystal, jet, bone, shell and pottery grave goods (S6; not independently confirmed) — if accurate, consistent with a rich elite burial rather than casual fill. Bernard Andreae (German Archaeological Institute) is reported to have identified the style as Roman, Severan-period (c. AD 193-235), via a secondhand quote ("Domenici 2000") that could not be located or independently checked for this record. Calixtlahuaca's Late Postclassic occupation ran to about AD 1530 (S4), so a Colonial-era intrusion into the deposit remains stratigraphically plausible on current evidence.
